title: Cutting our CI time from 18 minutes to 4
excerpt: How dependency caching, test sharding and a leaner Docker image made every pull request feel instant — with the numbers behind each change.

author.name: Priya Nair
author.bio: Priya leads DevOps and QA at the lab and maintains PipelineKit, the lab’s CI/CD template library.

body.text: In September, the median pull request in our lab waited 18 minutes for CI. Members had stopped waiting: they switched tasks, lost context and merged late. We decided to treat pipeline speed as a product problem.
Six weeks later the median is just under four minutes. None of the changes were exotic — they were measured, reviewed and shipped one pull request at a time.
Step one: measure before touching anything
We exported timings for every job across 300 recent runs. Installing dependencies and running the slowest test suite accounted for more than 70% of the wall-clock time.
If you cannot point at the slowest step with a number, you are guessing — and guessing is how pipelines get slower.
Step two: cache, shard, slim down
We cached the package manager store keyed on the lockfile, split the end-to-end suite into three shards, and moved to a multi-stage Docker build so only changed layers rebuild.

- uses: actions/cache@v4
  with:
    path: ~/.npm
    key: npm-${{ hashFiles('package-lock.json') }}

- run: npm test -- --shard=${{ matrix.shard }}/3
What we would repeat

items.t: — export timings and sort by cost.
— key them on lockfiles so stale caches never hide bugs.
— a CI change is production code and gets the same scrutiny.
— a dashboard keeps everyone invested.

body.text: The templates are open source inside PipelineKit if you want to reuse them in your own projects.

title: Writing tests first: lessons from HealthTrack API
excerpt: What happened when a team of beginners committed to test-driven development for an entire release cycle.

author.name: Marcus Lee
author.bio: Marcus is the lab’s tech lead and coaches teams on API design and testing.

body.text: The HealthTrack team agreed on one rule for the release cycle: no production code without a failing test first. The first two weeks were slow and frustrating.
By week four, the team was debugging less and refactoring more. Coverage climbed to 91% and the number of bugs reported after demos dropped to almost zero.
What changed

items.t: — a test naturally limits scope.
— reviewers read tests first to learn the intent.
— green tests meant safe changes.

body.text: The tests became our documentation, and the documentation never lied.
We still write exploratory code occasionally, but we throw it away and re-implement it test-first. It keeps the habit honest.

title: Our first open-source release: OpenKit UI 0.3
excerpt: Licences, changelogs, semantic versioning and the first outside contributor — a release diary.

author.name: Daniel Osei
author.bio: Daniel designs and builds accessible interfaces and leads the OpenKit UI team.

body.text: Publishing a package taught us that code is only half a release. The rest is a licence, a readme, a changelog, a contribution guide and a promise about versioning.
The release checklist

items.t: — MIT, added before the first public commit.
— keyboard and screen-reader checks on every component.
— breaking changes only in major versions.
— labelled tasks for newcomers.

body.text: Within a week, an outside contributor fixed a focus-ring bug. Reviewing a stranger’s pull request was a lesson in kind, precise feedback.

title: A code review checklist for beginners
excerpt: Reviewing code is a skill. Here is the one-page checklist every new lab member gets in week one.

author.name: Aria Chen
author.bio: Aria directs the lab and teaches the software engineering practice course.

body.text: Many beginners think review means finding mistakes. It is really about sharing context and keeping the codebase understandable.
Our one-page checklist

items.b: Does it do what the story says?
items.t: Read the description and acceptance criteria first.
Look for new or updated tests covering behaviour.
Names, small functions, and comments that explain why.
Input validation, secrets and permissions.
Ask questions, suggest alternatives, praise good work.

body.text: Review the code, not the person — and always leave one thing you liked.

title: From the lab to a first job: what alumni wish they knew
excerpt: Five alumni share how lab habits translated into their first engineering roles.

author.name: Aria Chen
author.bio: Aria directs the lab and teaches the software engineering practice course.

body.text: We asked five alumni what surprised them most in their first jobs. Their answers had little to do with syntax.

items.t: — clear pull request descriptions win trust.
— sprint planning in the lab prepared them for it.
— stuck for more than an hour? Pair up.

body.text: Their shared advice: keep a portfolio of merged pull requests, not just personal projects.

author.name: Marcus Lee
